newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan protesters vow island flotilla will sail.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan protesters vow island flotilla will sail.

text.p: More than 20 boats will sail to a chain of disputed East China Sea islands on October 6 as scheduled to rip down a lighthouse seen as a symbol of Japan's sovereignty claims, a Taiwanese organiser said on Friday.
"We will send people who are familiar with the waters, young and in good health condition, to land on the islands," Taipei county assemblyman Chin Chieh-shou said on state-funded radio.

More than 20 fishing boats from Taiwan and Hong Kong would take part, Chin said. It would be the biggest sea protest since July, when a Japanese right-wing group built a lighthouse and raised Japan's flag on the islands to assert Tokyo's sovereignty.
The uninhabited islands, known by the Chinese as the Diaoyus and the Japanese as the Senkakus, are claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan.

On Thursday, a voyage to the islands by a Hong Kong group ended in tragedy when its leader, David Chan, drowned after he and four other protesters jumped into the storm-whipped sea to defy Japan's claims.
Chin said his group would take extra precautions in the wake of Chan's death but would not back down.
"We will wear life vests and prepare for whatever is needed for this action," Chin said, adding that more than 200 people would join the protest to plant Taiwan's flag there.
Earlier this month Japanese coast guard ships twice blocked Chin's group from nearing the islands.
Separately, a group of Taiwanese ex-convicts also said they would swim to the Diaoyus to demolish the lighthouse when weather permits.

Japan took the disputed islands -- west of Japan's Okinawa island, northeast of Taiwan and east of China's southeastern Fujian coast -- as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and says there is no dispute to discuss.

China and Taiwan, separated by a civil war in 1949, say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and that the Diaoyus should have returned to Chinese rule after Japan's defeat at the end of World War Two.

China, keen to marshal patriotism stirred by the sovereignty row without offending Japanese investors, reiterated its call for Tokyo to restrain right-wing activists whose actions have whipped up Chinese nationalism against Japan.
The Taiwan government repeatedly called for calm in the simmering dispute, saying it planned to hold talks with Japan on fishery issues near the Diaoyus.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule in mid-1997 and many Hong Kong people see the dispute as a test of China's strength and integrity.
